lines: Tuesday, 16 April 2024
HAIRMAN:Good morning, everyone.
Thank you all for being here and for braving this
rather unusual Dubai weather, to be with us this
morning.
We're here for the merits, or evidentiary hearing in
Dubai Case Number 220035.  That's formerly known as case
number 35/2022, between Delta Al Emarate Building
Contracting LLC and LL Dubai Hotel LLC.
Before we begin, there are just a couple of
housekeeping items I would like to cover, if you don't
mind.
Firstly, just to confirm that provision has been
made for the swearing of the witnesses according to the
means that have been agreed between the parties, so we
don't have any delays with regard to holy books and
such?
R ORTEGA:  Yes.
R PATEL:  Yes.
HAIRMAN:Thank you.  Secondly, as we're all painfully
aware, we have quite a number of witnesses to get
through over the next four days.  The tribunal is, of
course, hopeful that we will be able to achieve
everything we have planned in the time that we have, and
looks forward to cooperation of counsel in doing so, and
in that regard, we will seek to encourage an efficient
conduct of these proceedings with a focus on the key
issues that parties believe they need to investigate in
witness examination, and ideally not as much focus on
other issues which of course we remain to be able to
deal with throughout the course of this proceeding.
With that, however, the tribunal did ask that the
parties each address in their opening submissions -- and
this has been done to some extent in the written
openings, for which we're grateful -- the claims, or the
positions of the parties as to the presence of either
new counterclaims in this proceeding, meaning
counterclaims that were not pleaded in the respondent's
submissions, or the extent to which the new evidence
which has been submitted in respect of counterclaims, is
evidence of -- is additional evidence going to pleaded
claims or not.
That's certainly an issue that we'll appreciate the
parties commenting on in their opening submissions.
Are there any comments from my colleagues?
Okay.  Could we start, then, just by having the
claimant briefly introduce us to the team at the table
and then we'll go to the respondent.
R ORTEGA:  Thank you, Mr Chairman.  My name is Fernando
Ortega.  You guys may know who I am already.  With us
today we have two representatives from the claimant, we
have Mr Moustafa and Mr Mahmoud, and then along with
those two we have our delay expert and our technical
expert with us, Dr Khaled and Mr Ahmed Abdelbakey.
Then with us remotely is Mr Lund.
HAIRMAN:Thank you very much.  For the respondent?
R PATEL:  I'm Sanjay Patel, I appear as lead advocate in
this arbitration.  Ms Handley appears with me as
counsel, and then Mr Hakim next to him of Fenwick
Elliott, Mr Varley next to him, Mr Sworder, MEP expert,
Mr Fletcher, our delay expert, Mr Moore, his assistant,
and then on the bank behind there we see Mr Stone of
Fenwick Elliott, and Mr Smith, the structural expert.
HAIRMAN:Thank you very much.
Are there any preliminary issues that the parties
wish to raise before we start the opening submissions?
R ORTEGA:  Yes.  We had a conversation in the hallway about
some of the preliminary issues we just want to raise as
housekeeping, at least from the claimant's side.  We
just want to put on the record that we did receive from
the respondent a power of attorney for both their new
counsel that have joined their, team and we have also
received the LAD authorisations confirming that they're
entitled, or at least they're allowed to, or permitted
by the DLAD to represent the party here in the
arbitration.
We just wanted to get that on record.  We didn't see
an email from Fenwick Elliott to the tribunal with the
powers of attorney, so just want to make that clear that
we did receive it and we have no objection to them
presenting respondent's case.
HAIRMAN:Thank you appreciated.  Thank you.
Any other?
R ORTEGA:  That's all for us.
HAIRMAN:For the respondent?
R PATEL:  There is one potential matter which is the status
of Mr Greenhough's supplementary report and
Mr Cornmell's supplementary report.
We read Mr Ortega's email over the weekend.
We are in a sense in your hands, chairman.  I don't
particularly want to take up time talking about that.
I think neither me nor Mr Ortega are necessarily
clear as to whether or not we are waiting for your
determination now, or whether you would appreciate
further submissions on it.
I'm in a position to address you on it if you would
like, but equally, having some level of procedural
direction as to how you would like us to address you is
probably the wisest course.
HAIRMAN:The tribunal has discussed the status of those
amended reports.  We view the position to be that there
has been, at least informally, an application for them
to be introduced and objection to that introduction.
As you're aware, when we dealt with the new evidence
from Mr Gill, we allowed that the tribunal would make
arrangements, whatever arrangements may be appropriate,
for the claimant to deal with the elements of Mr Gill's
statement that have been admitted.
At the moment, we have taken no view on the
admission of the amended expert reports and are
reserving the question of how to deal with them until
after we have heard from the parties this morning,
ideally, on their positions as to the question I framed
earlier, that the new claims versus new evidence of old
claims, and then at some point following that, the
tribunal will address the question of the new reports,
or the amended reports, but we'll do so in a way to, of
course, foster the availability of evidence that should
be before the tribunal without any, or going insofar as
possible avoiding any prejudice to the claimant in this
case, on account of the late or allegedly late
submission of that evidence.
So we'll reserve the position until we've heard from
the parties on these issues.
R PATEL:  Mr Chairman, obviously opening a case on the
facts is rather a different thing to addressing an
application to admit a supplementary expert report.
I for one would be grateful if we could deal with the
admission of Mr Greenhough's supplementary report and
Mr Cornmell's supplementary report as a discrete piece
of housekeeping, if that is agreeable to you.
HAIRMAN:That is what I -- apologies if I haven't been
clear.  That is what the tribunal intends.
R PATEL:  I see.
HAIRMAN:That we open the case that exists presently, and
we deal with -- when I say "we", the tribunal, having
heard that case opened, will further consider the
application and revert to the parties at a later point.
R PATEL:  I see.  May I address you now on that?  Or would
you prefer to delay that until after you have heard my
opening?
HAIRMAN:Let's proceed, subject to any contrary views,
with the parties' openings without being addressed on
the question of the new reports.
R PATEL:  I'm grateful.
R ORTEGA:  Sorry, one last thing, which was timekeeping.
You've asked the parties to keep their own time, a track
of their own time as well as the respondent.  Is it
possible that we can get maybe an established position
at the end of the day of what time has been taken by
both parties so we know moving forward.
HAIRMAN:That is certainly our intention.  At the end of
the day, if each time -- what we envision is that the
timekeepers for the two parties will meet and ideally
agree on the time that's been taken by each party.
Obviously the transcript serves as assistance in that.
To the extent there is a disagreement, which when
those arise generally arise as to whether an issue,
perhaps an interjection by the tribunal, belongs to one
party or the other, will come to the tribunal, or me in
the first instance, following the day, and we will make
a decision.
R ORTEGA:  Thank you.
HAIRMAN:Thank you.
R PATEL:  Final bit of housekeeping.  I understand that on
the live feed they can't hear us.  I say that not
because I expect you to be able to sort out the
audiovisual problems, but because someone at the back of
the room might be able to help.  Thank you.
HAIRMAN:Okay.
(Discussion off the record)
R PATEL:  Apparently they can hear now.
HAIRMAN:We have resolved the problem.
R ORTEGA:  Sorry, there are other people online?  This is
the first time I'm hearing this.  I know Mr Lund is
online, but is there other people on your team online?
HAIRMAN:I think they're assistants.
R PATEL:  Yes, the assistants, quantum expert, do you want
everyone online to be known?
R ORTEGA:  Yes, I would like to know who is online.  We
thought that they were going to be present here in the
hearing room.  That's what we understood from the email
message.
HAIRMAN:The understanding, I had, at least, was that they
would attend either in the room or virtually, depending
on the amount of space in the room.  But perhaps what
can happen is -- you have only Mr Lund online; is that
correct?
R ORTEGA:  Yes.
HAIRMAN:Could you tell us who is online on the
respondent's side?
R PATEL:  I am confident that Mr Greenhough, the quantum
expert, is online, I'm also confident that
Mr Postlewaight, his assistant, is online.  I'm
confident that Roma Patel, who is an associate with
Fenwick Elliott, is also online.  Obaid Kazmi of Kroll,
assistant to Mr Cornmell, I believe is online.
Mr Judge, another assistant to Mr Greenhough, is also
online, and Mr Kelly, assistant to Mr Sworder, is
online.  And I dare say Mr Cornmell is also online.
HAIRMAN:Perhaps what we can do, then, is we'll go forward
on the basis that everyone named is in attendance,
either virtually or physically.  If either party becomes
aware of a need for anyone else to attend, clearly
virtually, please announce that when you become aware.
R PATEL:  Thank you.
R ORTEGA:  Sounds good.
R HAFEZ:  If we could get an updated list at the end of the
day in the customary fashion, that would be very useful
for the award in due course.
R PATEL:  Certainly.
R COLE:  Just a small point.  Very helpfully I've got
a copy of the claimant's opening statement.  I don't
have a copy of the respondent's opening statement and
appendix, which I understood was going to be left for
me.
R HAKIM:  I'll just get a copy.
R COLE:  Thank you very much.
R ORTEGA:  Does the co-arbitrator need the copy now before
we start?
R COLE:  No, please go ahead.
Opening submissions by MR ORTEGA
R ORTEGA:  Thank you, gentlemen, for joining us today,
thank you everyone in the room for coming, especially
with the weather we're having today.
I'm going to briefly inform you or tell you what I'm
going to be going to in my presentation.  I start off
first by talking a brief overview about the dispute, and
then I will move to the claimant's claims, and I'll talk
about some of the defences being raised by the
respondent.  Then I'll go into the respondent's
counterclaims and then I will conclude.
This presentation is going to be a little bit longer
than what I was hoping for, primarily because we have
now received their opening note and this is effectively
their statement of defence and counterclaim.  There is
a lot of new issues that need to be covered, and I need
to cover these issues, and this is the only time we'll
be given that time.  So I'm going to probably go
a little bit more than one hour, just to give you an
idea of how long I'm going to take, but please during
that time if you have any questions or anything you want
to address to me while I'm going through, please feel
free to interrupt me, stop me, talk to me about
anything, I'm here to help you understand not only the
claimant's position, but also the respondent's position.
Like I said, we have received now this opening note
that has many new arguments that have been raised for
the first time, including a whole new delay section, or
a delay analysis supporting their case which we hadn't
seen before, in fact it was largely based on
Mr Fletcher's report, and all the evidence he submitted
through that report.
Now we have entered the 25th month of this dispute
and we're still trying to understand the respondent's
case.
It's clear with all these reports they're trying to
submit, especially over the weekend, all the additional
documents they are trying to submit over the weekend,
and the fact we were contacted by Mr Lund, Mr Greenhough
was actually trying to submit more evidence through him
a couple of days ago to support their claims.
We are at the hearing now, 25 months in, and we're
still trying to understand what the respondent is
actually claiming.
They've had a chance to submit five expert reports,
now trying to submit several more expert reports, and
they're still having difficulty trying to support their
case.  The reason why they're doing that now, they're
still trying to do this, because they can't prove their
case, they haven't yet proved it.  This is why they're
trying to submit all this evidence in.  If they
submitted their evidence in already, and they had their
expert report submitted with their evidence, or at least
had made submissions with their pleadings, we wouldn't
be worrying about submitting additional reports at this
time.
Again, I think we have said as many times in the
pleadings, that they failed to demonstrate that they
have -- failed to disclose key evidence in this
arbitration, and they failed to disclose, or actually
make arguments that they're entitled legally entitled
for the claims that they're actually making, and I'm
going to talk a little bit about that during my
presentation today.
Like I said, they have brought in five experts, now
they have brought in their assistants, for some unknown
reason, and now they have also brought a KC as well as
another barrister in the room, and primarily because
they're trying to convince you members of the tribunal,
that they don't have to pay the claimant the outstanding
moneys that they're owed to for the works that they
completed.  They don't have to pay, or they don't have
to prove that they suffered actual damages as required
under UAE law.  They can convince you, or they are
trying to convince you to hold the claimant longer under
this contract so they can continue to bring in more
defect claims against them.
More importantly, they're trying to convince you to
not allow the claimant to get its performance bond back.
Their claims are speculative, they go against UAE
law, legal commentary, court decisions and Sharia
principles of law, and ultimately what they're trying to
do with their alleged defects is change the hotel from
a 3 star hotel to a 4 star hotel.
Are these the signs of a respondent who's confident
in its case?  No, it's not.  It's a respondent who's
just trying to throw anything it can at the tribunal
with the hope that it can ultimately split the baby.
This dispute is very simple.  The claimant was engaged
to build a 3 star hotel.  This is said in the contract.
It's a Legoland Hotel built down in the Dubai Parks
area.  The claimant completed the works.  It was delayed
by the respondent in completing its works.  The TOC was
finally ready to be issued in March 2021.  It was signed
off by its own representatives, North25, in DEC, who are
not here.  However, the operator, who is not a party to
this contract, ordered the respondent not to issue the
TOC.  Why?  Because operator was not ready to receive
the hotel.  It did not have the licence to operate and
they needed the delay in the taking over.  That's why
you saw in April 2021 the operator issuing or creating
another, more issues for the claimant to deal with that
prevented the final taking-over certificate to be
issued.
The claimant, being a responsible contractor,
cleared out those issues, but then again in June 2021 we
saw the respondent issue more changes in, if I'm not
mistaken, variations as well.  The claimant cleared
those issues and under force, under threat of
litigation, the claimant was forced to issue a notice of
dispute in August.  They finally issued the taking-over
certificate in September 2021.
You can find that document at exhibit E28.
Now, what this effectively did was cause the defect
liability period to go from March all the way
to September.  That added six more months to the defect
liability period for the claimant to take
responsibility, or at least take care of any alleged
issues that they had in terms of trying to finalise the
building, which all those issues could have been dealt
with during the defect liability period.
There is no excuse for the TOC to be issued
in March 2021.
Now, I'm talking about this issue, I know we plead
this in the submissions and it sounds like a repeat, but
it's important to stress this because this is what this
case is about.
Members of the tribunal, you are tasked now to make
a decision on this specific issue first, because their
entire case walls around whether their defects were
actually a defect at that time of the taking-over
certificate.
It's important to understand what the taking-over
certificate says.  I'm going to put it here on record
just so the tribunal can reference it later:
"The respondent and its representatives ..." -- and
I am going to quote here, this is what the TOC says --
"... acknowledge and accepted that the works were
completed and taken over by the respondent in accordance
with the contract on the day of the taking over."
The TOC also says:
"North25 certifies that the works were completed to
a stage ready to be taken over by the employer in
accordance with the contract, except for any omissions,
outstanding work, defects, which the employer's
representative in its sole and absolute discretion, is
satisfied will not substantially affect the use of the
works for their intended purpose."
Now, the TOC also goes on to say that the
outstanding works and defects that they're referring to
are attached to the TOC in a punch list.  Those will be
completed within 30 days as instructed by North25.  Then
the claimant -- and also the claimant will be provided
access to be able to complete those snags, or those
punch lists.
The TOC is very clear here.  It says that the
employer and its representatives accepted the works and
confirmed that the punch list items will not affect the
intended use of the hotel.  They agree this.  They
signed this document.  They were fully aware of what
they're doing.
Now, the respondent disclosed that punch list in
this arbitration, and you can find that at hearing
bundle exhibit E541.
Now, what they disclose is only the NCR list.  They
didn't disclose the snag list.  I can tell you right
now, members of the tribunal, the claimant confirms that
it has closed out most if not all of those items.
The two parties who can confirm that, North25 and
DEC, they're not in this arbitration.  They decided not
to produce them, for some reason.  Now, again, what I'm
saying here is that this is important for the tribunal
to understand because the respondent's entire case is
based on these alleged defects that they're bringing
forward against the claimant, that they existed at that
time, and that was the reason why they withheld payment
to the claimant.  It wasn't because there was defects
that happened a year later, it was because these alleged
defects, the panic push button, or pad, they're trying
to claim now against the claimant, that existed at that
time, and that was the reason why they -- that was the
reason why they didn't have to pay the claimant the
first half of the retention which is required under the
contract.
That's their entire case.  But they have yet to
establish that.  What you're going to hear today from
the respondent's counsel is that no, we have all these
defects.  They handed us a defective hotel.  Right?
This is what you're going to hear from them today.  But
they haven't made the link yet, what defects that
they're claiming were actually a defect at that time, or
alleged defect at that time when the taking-over
certificate was issued and, if it was an alleged defect,
whether that can be actually remedied during the defect
liability period.
Now, the problem here they have here is that none of
those punch list items that I just mentioned in that
exhibit forms any of their defects.  In fact the snag
lists that were given, none of the defects which are
claimed in this arbitration are on those lists.  They
haven't gone into that, because they know they can't,
because none of those defects that they are claiming in
this arbitration are on that list.  In fact, many of
these defects raised -- in fact they just submitted
a couple more a couple of months ago, how -- they have
waited 37 months to then bring forward a defect claim.
The taking over certificate was issued
in September 2021, and 37 months later they're finally
realising there's a defect there?  They're using that
defect to say that they have the right to withhold the
payment, the first half of the retention.
This is the reason why we're here today.  This is
the reason why there's a dispute between the two
parties.
Now, just moving on here with a little bit of the
timeline, and some of the key documents here.  As per
the contract, once the TOC is issued, the first half
retention is automatically triggered to be paid.  This
is why you saw the claimant issue IPA number 30, which
is exhibit E31.
In that IPA you would see the payment or request for
payment for the first half of retention, and payment for
outstanding monies for works completed.
You have to understand the claimant is a contractor
here in the UAE, and they're the employer.  They are
represented by Dubai Holding.  Actually Dubai Holding is
sitting in the room here.  They have deep pockets.  The
claimant is a contractor.  Contractor needs money to be
able to continue on operating.  Depended highly on cash
flow.  It needed to pay its subcontractors to complete
the snags and complete any potential defects that they
might have, and this is why they're very dependent at
that time to get that first half retention to be able to
pay the subcontractors.
But they didn't happen.  Problems start happening
with their subbies and as well as their suppliers, and
in particular their MEP subcontractor who we are, or the
claimant is now bringing forward a subcontract claim, or
at least bringing the claim against them, against the
claimant, by the MEP subcontractor, and I can confirm to
you now that that MEP subcontractor has now filed
arbitration case against the claimant because of their
delays.
After that, after the IPA, then we get North25
certifying the payment, and the payment certificate, and
you can find the email where the payment certificate at
exhibit E22.
This document is also important because if you read
the text of that payment certificate, it places no
conditions, no contracharges, no payment withheld, no
offsets, nothing there, there's no defects identified,
there's nothing in there that says that they are
deducting monies for alleged defects because of defects
raised before TOC was issued, during TOC was issued, or
any of the items on the punch list.
It doesn't say any of that.  In fact, what it says,
and I'm going to quote here, just to put it on the
record, it says "we confirm", meaning we meaning North25
who's required under the contract to certify payment:
"We confirm and certify that the amount for payment
to the claimant on this certificate includes, for this
stage of works [which is the final TOC stage],
satisfactory completed by the claimant confirming that
the works have been completed in accordance with the
contract."
That means the specifications, that means the design
that they were asked to build under, and the other thing
that's important to understand here, members of the
tribunal, there was no objection by the respondent at
that time when they issued that payment certificate.
There was no claim for defects by the respondent.  There
was a bunch of snag lists that were circulated and you
had the NCR list, or the punch lists.  That was the only
thing that is there.  You don't see anything about
waterproofing, you don't see anything about all the
other MEP claims that they're trying to make in this
arbitration.
After that, members of the tribunal, you see the
claimant then issuing its tax invoice for the amount
certified by North25 as per the terms of the contract.
And as per the perms of the contract, 21 days after the
PC is issued, that payment is due.
Then again, respondent has failed to make that
payment.  Why?  We don't know.  There is no reason why.
Maybe you might be told today why they didn't do it at
that time.  But you're going to hear them say no, no, it
was because all these waterproofing issues, all these
panic push pad or whatever they are trying to claim,
what are the MEP defects, it was because of that we were
entitled to withhold payments.
Now, the claimant issued notifications to the
respondent about the payment.  They did it so on two
times.  They did on 23 November where they identified:
If you don't pay us on time, or if you don't pay us
money, we're going to suspend works in 42 days.  After
that it was 16 December, 2021 where again they were
reminded of the payment issue and again they were going
to suspend at the end of the 42 days, which was going to
be on 5 January.  Again, no response from the
respondent.
Then on 5 January came around, the contractor
exercised its right under the contract to suspend.
Again, the important point -- another important note
here is that the claimant during this entire time, ever
since the taking-over certificate was issued, all the
way up to the day it suspended, it continued completing
the snag list, it continued taking care of any other
issues raised or any changes to the specifications
raised by the respondent or the operator, it continued
to do that without payment.
Now, because they didn't respond to that notice,
them suspending, that forced the claimant then to again
exercise its rights, and you saw in February -- if I'm
not mistaken, 24 February, you see that the claimant
issuing a notice of intention to commence arbitration,
with the hope that that might trigger the respondent to
make payment, or at least come to the table and discuss
the payment issue.
You can find that document at exhibit E36.
Again, no response.  The claimant was blessed with
no other choice but then to start arbitration
proceedings that following month in 11 March 2022.
We finally heard from the respondent on 16 March
after they commenced arbitration, where then at that
time for the first time they accused the claimant of not
completing its works on time and -- on time, but then
they did this, though, after they received a report from
their own representative confirming that the claimant
did not -- was entitled to the extension of time and did
not delay the works.  It was actually the respondent who
delayed the works.
That's DEC.  Where is DEC now?  They're not here.
They're a key witness for them, they're their
representative on site, and they didn't have them here
as a witness.
Like I said, it is not only DEC, it's also North25
who not only confirmed the works were satisfied, but are
a key witness here.  They can speak to every single
issue that's impacting this dispute, including their
alleged defects.  And any workmanship issues that
they're alleging, DEC, North25 can speak to that.  But
they're not here today.
DEC Mr Farrag, we tried to bring in Mr Farrag into
the arbitration because he wanted to speak his mind, but
he didn't want to choose sides between the two parties.
But we were denied that.
North25, Mr Alistair, Mr David -- North25 is
actually owned by Dubai Holding, they could easily bring
them here, but they didn't bring them.  They can speak
directly.  If there was such issues with defects North25
could confirm that to you, members of the tribunal.  But
they don't have him as a witness.  There's a reason why.
Because they wouldn't support the respondent's case.
The other key witness that's not here is Mr Remi Ishak.
He's the CEO of the company, he's the one who issued the
TOC.  He signed the TOC and confirmed that the works
were satisfactory.  If he was not -- if the respondent's
confident in its case and was certain that these alleged
defects were such an issue, he would be the one sitting
at the table right here telling you guys that:  The TOC
was not proper, and the works were not satisfied, and
I only signed it for another reason.
Whatever that reason is, we don't know.  He can
confirm that that the works were not completed and the
defects that they're raising are an issue for the hotel
before TOC and after the TOC, if we are to believe the
respondent's case.  But he's not here to tell you that.
He signs all the letters, he issues, if not mistaken he
issued power of attorney, but he's not here to represent
or at least to speak to the members of the tribunal
about the issues in dispute.
That tells you a lot about their case.  That tells
you a lot about what they think about their case in
terms of support.  In fact, we have no witness from
their side here.  They brought Mr Graham Gill.  At that
time he was working for the operator.  He wasn't working
for the respondent.  They hired him later to prepare the
defects claim.  No one from their side is appearing in
this arbitration, and that should tell you a lot about
their case, that should tell you they're not confident
in their case, and this is why you see all these last
minute defect claims they're trying to submit evidence
that could have been submitted with their statement of
defence and counterclaim, but they're now doing it now,
because they don't have trust in their case.
We disclosed, we asked for that email to be issued
with their conversation with DEC, not because we were
going to make accusations at them because they were
trying to make accusations against the claimant about
producing a false record or a false email and report.
We weren't going to do that for that purpose.  We did
that to show the members of the tribunal that in October
when we submitted that application to bring Mr Farag
in's, they were on the phone with DEC asking them about
the issues in the dispute, and then from that point
forward, we were told by Mr Farrag that they were no
longer able to speak to us about this case.  They're
intentionally telling DEC not to speak to us anymore
about the issues around this case.
Again, is that a respondent who's confident in its
case?  No, it's not.
Just to wrap up this overview of the dispute.
I just want to say that the claimant completed its job
under the contract.  It delivered a 3 star hotel which
the respondent sitting here today is profiting from.
They achieved over 97 per cent capacity, or occupancy, I
should say, during the peak times, last year in
particular, where they had in use over 240 rooms, and
a document to prove that is at exhibit E540.  Again,
there is no reason why the TOC couldn't be issued
in March 2021.  The respondent stated in this
arbitration that its intention to hold the claimant
